meta.title: Who really said "I Would Rather Go To Bed With That Woman Stark Naked Than With Ulysses S. Grant in Full Military Regalia"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Flagg — his 1946 memoir reports Mark Twain saying it of Adelina Patti. The Lillian Russell "full military regalia" wording is in no Twain text.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I Would Rather Go To Bed With That Woman Stark Naked Than With Ulysses S. Grant in Full Military Regalia'?
meta.ogDescription: Twain's notebook and Flagg's 1946 memoir both name Adelina Patti and "full uniform." Lillian Russell and "full military regalia" came later, and unsourced.

answer.label: Not James Montgomery Flagg — he reported it of Mark Twain
answer.authorDates: 1835–1910 · American writer and humorist (the reported speaker)
answer.sourceLine: Flagg is the memoirist, not the wit. The wording that survives in print comes from Flagg’s 1946 autobiography Roses and Buckshot, page 169, where he retells a story he got second-hand from Maisie La Shelle: Mark Twain, watching Adelina Patti at the old Academy, whispers to William Dean Howells that he’d rather sleep with that woman stark naked than with General Grant in full uniform. The popular form — Lillian Russell, and “Ulysses S. Grant in full military regalia” — is a later reshaping that Boller and George list among fake Twain quotes ↗, and even Twain’s own notebook records the joke as somebody else’s.

source.excerpt: Flagg, retelling a story he had from Maisie La Shelle: Twain and William Dean Howells sat in the front row at the old Academy while Adelina Patti sang; Howells caught the leer in Twain’s eye and asked about it. Twain’s answer, as Flagg prints it: “I would rather sleep with that woman stark naked, than with General Grant in full uniform!”
trail: 1889–90 — Mark Twain’s notebook, later printed in Mark Twain’s Notebooks & Journals, Volume III (University of California Press), pages 537–38, carries a Patti version that Twain frames as a report of someone else’s remark, per Quote Investigator ↗.

1942 — a theatre review collected in George Jean Nathan’s Theatre Book of the Year, 1942–1943 runs a Lillian Russell variant about looking at rather than sleeping with her, one of the citations assembled by Quote Investigator ↗.
1946 — James Montgomery Flagg prints the “that woman stark naked … General Grant in full uniform” anecdote on page 169 of Roses and Buckshot ↗, crediting the story to Maisie La Shelle.
1989 — Paul F. Boller Jr. and John George file the modern Lillian Russell wording under Mark Twain in They Never Said It ↗, page 123, and state that it is found nowhere in his writings.
source.excerptNote: Note what is not here: no “go to bed with,” no “Ulysses S. Grant,” no “full military regalia,” and no Lillian Russell. Every one of those is a later retelling’s improvement on the line.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for the popular wording, because no source contains it. The two texts that do carry versions of the line are both modern publications: Flagg’s Roses and Buckshot (G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1946) and the University of California Press edition of Twain’s notebooks — each published well after 1930 and therefore not to be treated as public domain. Twain’s own pre-1931 published books are public domain, but this sentence is not in them.

author.name: Mark Twain
author.heading: Who the joke actually belongs to
author.bio: Samuel Langhorne Clemens (November 30, 1835 – April 21, 1910), writing as Mark Twain, was an American writer, humorist and essayist — and the single most magnetic name in English for orphaned one-liners. This one has a real thread back to him: a passage in his own notebook, written between May 1889 and August 1890, sets the quip beside Adelina Patti and General Grant. But Twain phrased it as a report of someone else’s remark, and Quote Investigator concludes he may have been writing down a joke he heard rather than one he made.

cite.sourceCitation: James Montgomery Flagg, Roses and Buckshot (New York: G. P. A related passage stands in Mark Twain’s Notebooks & Journals, Volume III (1883–1891) (Berkeley: University of California Press), 537–38, cited by Quote Investigator. The popular “Lillian Russell … full military regalia” form is listed as unsourced in Paul F. Boller Jr. and John George, They Never Said It (New York: Oxford University Press, 1989), 123.

Flagg's 1946 memoir "Roses and Buckshot" (p. 169) prints the line as a second-hand anecdote about Mark Twain, said of the soprano Adelina Patti: "I would rather sleep with that woman stark naked, than with General Grant in full uniform!" The popular "Lillian Russell ... Ulysses S. Grant in full military regalia" wording appears nowhere in Twain's writings (Boller & George, They Never Said It, 1989, p. 123). — Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Three wrong labels on one joke
misattribution.intro: This line travels with almost everything about it mislabelled — the speaker, the woman, and the wording. Here is what each source actually supports.

items.why: Flagg’s Roses and Buckshot is where the “that woman stark naked” wording is printed, but Flagg puts it in Mark Twain’s mouth and states that Maisie La Shelle told him the story years after the fact. Page 169 of the scanned 1946 edition ↗ shows the anecdote as Flagg framed it.

Boller and George put the Lillian Russell form of the popular sentence under Twain in They Never Said It and dismiss it: the remark can be found nowhere in Twain’s writings — page 123 of the 1989 edition ↗.

The early records name Adelina Patti. Russell appears in retellings from the 1940s onward — a 1942 theatre review, a 1975 Wall Street Journal column, a 1998 book of San Francisco literary lore — all gathered by Quote Investigator ↗, which calls the substitution a later modification.

Twain’s own notebook entry begins “He said” — he is writing down someone else’s remark. Quote Investigator ↗ notes it is possible Twain heard the quip and did not construct it himself, and Evan Esar filed it as a stock Patti gag.

misattribution.truthLine: What is documented is narrow: Twain’s notebook, written between 1889 and 1890, records a Patti-and-Grant version phrased as another person’s remark, and Flagg’s 1946 memoir prints a second-hand anecdote of Twain saying it aloud. Neither text is the sentence people quote — see Quote Investigator’s citation trail ↗.

context.heading: How a whisper became a slogan
lead: The joke has a fixed shape and a swappable cast. In the oldest recorded forms the woman is Adelina Patti (1843–1919), the operatic superstar of the age, and the general is in “full uniform.” Twain’s notebook has it that way, and so does Flagg’s memoir. The Patti form was still circulating as an anonymous gag decades later: Evan Esar’s 1978 Comic Encyclopedia prints it as an oft-repeated Patti gag with no mention of Twain at all, per Quote Investigator’s survey of the citations ↗.

Then the cast changes. By 1942 a theatre review is running a Lillian Russell version, and by the 1970s the line has hardened into the crisp, quotable sentence people repeat today — “go to bed with,” a full presidential name, “full military regalia.” None of those upgrades appears in the early records. They are the polish a joke acquires from being retold, and the polish is exactly what makes the modern version unfindable in any primary text.
context.detailsSummary: Why Flagg’s name gets attached at all
detailsBody: Flagg (1877–1960) is a famous name in his own right — the illustrator behind the 1917 “I Want YOU for U.S. Army” Uncle Sam poster. He knew Twain and painted him. So when reference works cite Roses and Buckshot as the place the anecdote is printed, the citation and the credit are easy to confuse, and Flagg quietly slides from witness to wit.

He was not even a witness. Flagg says plainly that Maisie La Shelle told him the story years after the fact, and he published it in 1946 — decades after Twain’s death in 1910. It is a second-hand anecdote in a memoir, which is worth something, but it is not a transcript.
context.pull: Every retelling made the sentence better and the provenance worse.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces the quip to Adelina Patti (not Lillian Russell), cites Mark Twain's notebook written between May 1889 and August 1890 (Notebooks & Journals Vol. III, pp. 537-38) reading 'He said he would rather sleep with Adelina Patti without a stitch of clothes on than with General Grant in full uniform', cites James Montgomery Flagg's 1946 Roses and Buckshot p.169 for the second-hand Twain/Howells anecdote, notes the 1942 Nathan review, 1975 WSJ, 1978 Esar, 1989 Boller & George and 1998 Rathmell variants, and concludes the Lillian Russell substitution is a later modification and Twain may have heard rather than invented the quip.

The scanned 1946 edition of James Montgomery Flagg's Roses and Buckshot contains, on page 169, the passage in which Maisie La Shelle's story has Twain and Howells at the old Academy hearing Adelina Patti, with Twain saying 'I would rather sleep with that woman stark naked, than with General Grant in full uniform!'

Boller and George's They Never Said It (1989), page 123, lists under Mark Twain (1835-1910) the quote 'I would rather go to bed with Lillian Russell stark naked than with Ulysses S. Grant in full military regalia' and states 'This remark, unfortunately, can be found nowhere in Twain's writings.'
Open Library's catalogue record for ISBN 0520033833 is Mark Twain's Notebooks & Journals, Volume III (1883-1891), published by the University of California Press, 892 pages.

James Montgomery Flagg lived June 18, 1877 - May 27, 1960, was an American artist and illustrator, created the 1917 'I Want YOU for U.S. Army' Uncle Sam poster, and published his autobiography Roses and Buckshot in 1946 through G. P. Putnam's Sons.
Adelina Patti (19 February 1843 - 27 September 1919) was a celebrated operatic soprano who made her operatic debut at the Academy of Music in New York City in 1859.
Mark Twain was the pen name of Samuel Langhorne Clemens (November 30, 1835 - April 21, 1910), an American writer, humorist and essayist.

The English Wikiquote page for Mark Twain contains no entry for this quip in any section - its raw wikitext has no mention of Lillian Russell, Adelina Patti, or 'full military regalia' (checked, negative result; not cited on the page).
